deck: 20 Head First Java::01 Breaking the Surface

cards.front: How many main() methods does a Java application need?
cards.back: One — and it is one per application, not one per class
cards.extra: Every application needs at least one class and at least one main method. Other classes can be completely main-free; the JVM looks for the single entry point it was told to start.
cards.example:
class App {
    public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("one entry point"); }
}
// other classes can declare main too, but an application runs one main()

cards.front: The JVM is told to run a class. How does it find where execution begins?
cards.back: It loads that class, then looks for a method written exactly as public static void main(String[] args)
cards.extra: The signature must match exactly — this is why main(String args) or a missing static compiles but the launcher refuses to start, with an error about no main method.
cards.example:
class LaunchTarget {
    public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("entry point found"); }
}
// JVM loads the class, then looks for public static void main(String[] args)

cards.front: Where in a class may a statement appear?
cards.back: Inside a method body — never directly in the class body
cards.extra: The nesting is fixed: source file → class → method → statement. A statement sitting between fields is a compile error, because a class may only contain declarations.
cards.example:
class Legal {                 // a statement belongs inside a method body
    void run() { int x = 1; System.out.println(x); }   // valid here
}
// int y = 2; directly in the class body would not compile

cards.front: What does one .java source file typically contain?
cards.extra: A tiny application can be a single class. The class, and every method in it, must sit inside curly braces — braces define what belongs to what.

cards.front: What type must a Java conditional test evaluate to?
cards.extra: Java has no truthiness: an int is not a condition. while (x) is a compile error where while (x > 0) is not — the test has to be a real question.
cards.example:
int x = 1;
boolean test = x > 0;
if (test) { System.out.println("ok"); }

cards.front: Which operator assigns, and which compares for equality?
cards.extra: if (x = 3) does not compile in Java for that reason — an assignment yields a value, not a boolean. This is one place Java protects you from a classic C bug.
cards.example:
int x = 5;
boolean same = (x == 5);
x = 6;
System.out.println(same + " " + x);

cards.front: What delimits a code block such as a loop or method body?
cards.extra: Everything between the braces belongs to the block. Indentation is for humans — the braces decide scope, which is why code that looks aligned can still be inside the wrong block.
cards.example:
if (true) {   // opening brace starts the block
    int n = 1;   // statement inside the block
}   // closing brace ends it

cards.front: A while test is false on the very first check. What happens?
cards.back: The body never runs; execution continues at the first line after the loop
cards.extra: The test is evaluated before every iteration, including the first. That is the difference from do-while, whose body always runs once.
cards.example:
int x = 0;
while (x > 0) { System.out.println("never"); }
System.out.println("after loop");

cards.front: What does javac do about errors before it produces a .class file?
cards.back: It refuses to compile until the source is free of errors it can detect
cards.extra: javac checks the source and stops with an error list instead of emitting bytecode. This is why type errors and typos surface before anything runs, while casting mistakes can still escape to runtime.
cards.example:
// javac writes no .class file while errors remain in the source
// `int x = ;` is an error — fix it before compiling
int x = 1;   // clean source compiles

cards.front: What property of bytecode lets one compiled program run on any device that has a JVM?
cards.back: Bytecode is platform-independent — only the JVM is machine-specific
cards.extra: The compiler targets the JVM instruction set, not a CPU. Each device supplies its own JVM, which translates the same bytecode into what its hardware understands.
cards.example:
// Bytecode is platform-independent; only the JVM is machine-specific.
class Portable {
  static void run() { System.out.println("same bytecode"); }
}

cards.front: Why does Java code written in 1996 still run on a current JVM?
cards.back: Backward compatibility is a deliberate promise of the platform
cards.extra: New versions add APIs and language features without removing the old ones, which is why the book teaches old idioms first: you will meet 20-year-old Java in real codebases.
cards.example:
class OldCode {                  // Java written in 1996 still runs on a current JVM
    void run() { System.out.println("still runs"); }
}
// Backward compatibility is a deliberate promise of the platform

cards.front: In String[] pets = {"Fido", "Zeus", "Bin"}; at which index is "Zeus"?
cards.extra: The first element is index 0, so a three-element array runs 0…2. Picking a random element means 0 … length-1, which is why the idiom is random.nextInt(pets.length).
cards.example:
String[] pets = {"Fido", "Zeus", "Bin"};
System.out.println(pets[1]);   // Zeus — arrays are zero-based
System.out.println(pets[0]);   // Fido

cards.front: What does pets.length return for an array?
cards.back: The number of elements — a field, not a method
cards.extra: No parentheses: pets.length is correct, pets.length() is not. Strings differ: s.length() is a method call.
cards.example:
String[] pets = {"Fido", "Zeus", "Bin"};
System.out.println(pets.length);   // 3 — a field, not a method like length()
